title: For Some New Voters, a Ballot Carries the Whole Family
summary: Many young voters worry about homes, student loans, and starting a family. But for young people from immigrant families, voting can feel even bigger. Nicole Solis-Sison, 34, moved from the Philippines when she was seven, after her family fled and asked for asylum. After more than twenty years in the immigration system, she became an American citizen earlier this year. Now she is voting for the first time in New York City. Juan Escalante, 37, moved from Venezuela when he was 11. He learned in high school that he was undocumented. Under a program called Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals, he became his family's first college graduate and, in 2025, its first American citizen. Now he votes in his first general election in California. Deisy Espana, 24, was born in Wisconsin, but her parents came from Mexico and were undocumented. She says she is voting for her parents, who cannot vote. Leydi Gonzalez, 23, of Texas says she is voting for her family's security.
why_it_matters: Just like your family may make big decisions together, a vote can carry the hopes of parents and relatives who cannot vote themselves.

background_read: Voting is how citizens choose leaders and help decide what happens in their communities.
For people from immigrant families, becoming a citizen can take a long time, and only citizens can vote.
That is why a first vote can feel like a big moment for a whole family, not just for one person.

WHERE: In New York City, California and Texas, where these new voters are casting their votes
WHY: Because they waited years to become citizens, or have parents who cannot vote, so their vote also speaks for their family
